newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Arabs seek U.N. Assembly session after U.S. veto.
newsitem.headline: Arabs seek U.N. Assembly session after U.S. veto.

text.p: Arab countries pressed for an emergency meeting of the 185-nation General Assembly after the United States vetoed a Security Council resolution calling on Israel to abandon plans for a new Jewish neighbourhood in mainly Arab East Jerusalem.

The vote in the 15-nation council late on Friday was 14 in favour, with only the United States opposing the resolution, sponsored by four of its European Union allies -- Britain, France, Portugal and Sweden.

A similar resolution is certain to win overwhelming backing in the Assembly, where there is no veto. Though its decisions are a gauge of world opinion, they do not carry the weight of council resolutions and are not binding.
The United States was among nearly 50 countries that criticised the Israeli move during a two-day council debate.
But Ambassador Bill Richardson, the new U.S. envoy, said the council was not an appropriate forum for issues now under discussion between Israel and the Palestinians.

He also said the resolution made "sweeping statements concerning the legal status of Israeli settlements," which Israel and the Palestinians had agreed would be among so-called "permanent status" issues to be discussed during forthcoming talks.

The current chairman of the Arab group, which initiated the council debate, ambassador Nasser bin Hamad al-Khalifa of Qatar, said an emergency session of the Assembly would be summoned as soon as possible.
"We will achieve a solution which is accepted by the majority of the human race," he said.

"The Security Council, with the veto power, is becoming a dictatorial instrument. The General Assembly is the only democratic institution within the United Nations, representing the majority of the human race," he told reporters.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, said the U.S. veto would have a negative impact on the Middle East peace process.

There had been a "clear, unanimous, strong international position which was prevented from being translated into a resolution because of a veto which was cast by the United States of America," he said.
The veto "might be misunderstood by the Israelis... as some kind of green light or yellow light for them to proceed with their project," al-Kidwa added.

The veto followed a council debate on Wednesday and Thursday sparked by Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem that it captured during the 1967 Middle East war.

The site is called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians. Israel regards the Holy City as its undivided capital while the Palestinians see East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
The veto was the 71st cast by the United States and the first by Richardson, who last month succeeded Madeleine Albright, now U.S. secretary of state, as the American U.N. representative.
The previous U.S. veto was in May 1995, to block a resolution calling on Israel to rescind the expropriation of 131 acres (53 hectares) of Arab land in East Jerusalem.
Russia has used its veto 116 times, Britain on 30 occasions, France 18, and China 3.
The defeated council resolution would have expressed deep concern over Israel's decision to "initiate new settlement activities in the Jabal Abu Ghneim area in East Jerusalem."

It would have called on "the Israeli authorities to refrain from all actions or measures, including settlement activities, which alter the facts on the ground, pre-empting the final status negotiations, and have negative implications for the Middle East peace process."

The resolution also would have called on Israel to abide by its obligations under the Fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians in time of war, which bars settlements in occupied territory.
